name: Fatima Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a small payment software team at a tech company. I have a master’s degree, and I start by checking overnight charge failures before we change code. I like finding the odd mistake everyone else missed; I dislike that team lead responsibility comes with relatively low pay and very little saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I’d say the tools are useful for basic test code that sets up checks, but the product still needs people who know its customers. I already use a coding assistant every day, and I make the final call on a release.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My pay is low for a team lead with a master’s, and I have less than a month of bills saved. A quiet AI story still leaves me one broken laptop away from borrowing money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d keep leading the payment service team and ask for a pay review after our next release. In the first year I’d put the first extra 200 a month into an emergency account if the review comes through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel relieved about the code, but the rent would still sit in my stomach. I like knowing the work is mine to answer for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say if the pay review fails?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep the release work steady and ask our director which milestones would earn the rise. I wouldn’t put a made-up 200 into a savings plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would hear the money worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister Lena knows because she lent me 80 for a train fare last spring. I would tell her I’m trying to stop that happening again.

say: I say **coding assistants** save routine test time while I still own the release decision.
I say our **payment service** needs people who understand customer mistakes and old systems.
think: My **team lead pay** is low for the responsibility I carry.
I have **under one month saved**, so an ordinary equipment bill feels dangerous.
do: **Keep leading** the payment service release and request a pay review afterward.
**Save 200 monthly** from a raise, if our director approves one.
feel: **Relieved** about the work, but tense about rent.
S0.quote: A quiet AI story still leaves me one broken laptop away from borrowing money.
fieldNote: Her public confidence in **human judgment** is genuine; routine coding help already belongs in her day.
The strongest pressure is **thin savings** and low pay, even if AI stalls.

steps.text: Keep leading the payment service release at the tech company
Deposit 200 monthly from an approved raise into emergency savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my team to learn the tools and check every generated change before it reaches a customer. The easy tickets might disappear, but someone must decide what a broken payment means.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think management could use faster code to freeze hiring and squeeze my team. Being the best debugger in the room doesn’t protect my salary if the room gets smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I’d document the payment failures only I know and train the others to audit AI output. I’d apply now for better paid lead roles in other cities, but I’d only pay to travel once an interview is confirmed; there are few openings nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be keyed up, not frozen. My hands know how to work with AI, but my bank balance cannot carry a long job hunt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a junior developer whose easy tickets vanish?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d give her one real incident each week and make her explain why the fix is safe. I cannot promise her a job, but I can give her a record of decisions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI daily; what part would you still distrust?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A generated fix can pass tests and still charge the same customer twice. I would keep the final payment checks with a named engineer.

say: I tell colleagues to **learn the tools** and check generated changes before customers see them.
I say **payment mistakes** still need accountable people, even when code arrives faster.
think: I fear management may **freeze hiring** and ask a smaller team to ship more.
My **debugging skill** may not protect pay when headcount shrinks.
do: **Document payment failures** and teach teammates to audit generated fixes now.
**Apply now** for distant lead roles, paying to travel only after an interview is confirmed.
feel: **Keyed up** about shrinking jobs, yet able to act.
S1.quote: Being the best debugger in the room doesn’t protect my salary if the room gets smaller.
fieldNote: Daily AI use gives her a **practical response**, including training colleagues on real failures.
The gap between public instruction and private fear is **headcount**, not code quality.

steps.text: Teach payment engineers to audit AI generated fixes using past failures
Apply now for distant lead roles and travel only for confirmed interviews

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In a meeting I’d say no one should pretend an AI system is a person who can own a billing error. I’d ask management to tell us which releases still need a human signature.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, full thinking AI by 2028 could write, test and plan most of my job for less. Robots in 2031 barely matter to my desk work. I might be leading a team that no longer has a payroll.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d cancel the new car lease I was planning and send two applications to product safety teams this week. If full AGI arrives in 2028, I’d take paid incident work if it exists and a contract covers rent and health cover; I wouldn’t quit for an unpaid course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be scared enough to wake at four. I can move quickly, but I cannot buy two years of breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill changes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I own an older car, so I’d keep it rather than sign the new lease I had planned. That would leave about 160 a month in my account while I still have wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If an employer offers only a short contract, do you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take a six-month paid contract if the rate covers rent and health cover. I would not call it security, but cash has to keep moving.

say: I want **human sign-off** to remain clear when a billing error reaches a customer.
I want management to name which **payment releases** require an engineer who accepts responsibility.
think: I think **full AGI in 2028** could replace most coding, testing and planning I lead.
I expect later **robots** to add little to my desk job already exposed in 2028.
do: **Cancel the planned lease** and keep my older car, leaving about 160 monthly while wages continue.
**Apply this week** to paid product safety teams and seek incident work if it exists after 2028.
**Accept a short contract** only if its rate covers rent and health cover.
feel: **Scared** and waking early, despite knowing how to move.
S2.quote: I might be leading a team that no longer has a payroll.
fieldNote: Her **2028 risk** is direct because nearly all of her work is thinking work.
She rejects unpaid retraining because **rent** and thin savings rule out a gap in wages.

steps.text: Cancel the planned new lease and keep the older owned car
Apply to paid product safety and incident roles if openings exist
Accept a paid incident contract only if it covers rent and health cover

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years gives us time to make a real plan, and the company should publish it. I’d still insist that humans sign off on payments as long as they carry legal blame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I’d be less afraid than in 2028, but this is still my whole trade under pressure. The robots arriving around 2034 do not grant software developers three extra safe years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I’d ask to lead our fraud review project and save the raise if I get one. If AGI arrives in 2031, I’d move toward customer dispute and audit work if paid openings exist, rather than count on coding alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious, with a timetable I can actually write down. Five years lets me test whether another role pays before I leave this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know the fraud role was real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the director for a written project budget and my name as lead. A hopeful chat in the kitchen is not a job plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your family cover a gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister Lena would help in an emergency, but she has her own rent. I want my own cash buffer, not an invisible loan from her.

say: I say five years permits a **company plan** with named roles and deadlines.
I want **human signatures** to match human responsibility for payment errors.
think: My **software trade** still faces full thinking AI in 2031.
I know later **robots** do not postpone that risk for developers.
do: **Request a funded** fraud review lead assignment from our director this year.
**Save any raise** from that assignment in an emergency account.
**Apply for paid** dispute or audit openings after 2031, if any remain.
feel: **Anxious**, though a five-year timetable gives room to test options.
S3.quote: The robots arriving around 2034 do not grant software developers three extra safe years.
fieldNote: She treats the **2031 date** as the deadline for coding work, regardless of later robots.
A written **fraud budget** matters more to her than verbal reassurance.

steps.text: Request a funded fraud review lead assignment from the director
Deposit any fraud assignment raise into emergency savings
Apply for paid dispute or audit openings if available after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell younger developers that a decade is enough time to choose carefully, not a reason to stop learning. Our team should keep records of where automated changes fail customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could build savings and become a trusted person for payment disputes by 2036. I also know full thinking AI may do that reasoning too, so I wouldn’t sell it as a permanent shelter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I’d learn to use AI to check payment reversals for double charges, and take one customer dispute shift each month to learn the real complaints. Over the next ten years I’d build a six-month cash buffer if pay allows; in the first year after 2036, I’d take a paid dispute role only if people still need one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel steadier about the long deadline, but rent and less than one month saved still worry me now. I have time to make a choice before fear makes it for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up to build that buffer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep my current small flat instead of moving to a nicer one if my pay rises. The difference could fund the buffer without making every week miserable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if dispute work is automated too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d look at paid roles with customer responsibility, and I might still have to change fields. I cannot name a safe profession ten years ahead.

say: I say a **decade** gives our payment developers time to learn, test options and choose carefully.
I want us to record where **automated changes** hurt customers.
think: I could build a **six-month buffer** before 2036, if my pay holds.
I know even customer disputes may be **automated**, so no role is guaranteed shelter.
do: **Learn an AI check** for double charges on payment reversals and work one customer dispute shift monthly.
**Stay in my flat** and save if pay allows, then seek paid dispute work if openings remain after 2036.
feel: **Steadier about 2036**, but still anxious about current rent and thin savings.
S4.quote: I cannot name a safe profession ten years ahead.
fieldNote: Her new **AI check** for payment reversals is specific learning, while her dispute shifts teach customer problems.
She names **uncertainty** about whether dispute work survives; her move depends on a paid opening after AGI arrives.

steps.text: Learn an AI check for double charges on payment reversals
Keep the current flat and save toward six months of expenses if pay allows
Apply for paid customer dispute roles if openings remain in 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the thinking work could go before I have a cash buffer. A funded paid transition role in customer accountability, with a written budget and enough income for rent, would help more than a promise about future skills.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask how a team lead tells people their jobs may vanish. I would want the company to tell them directly, early, with real dates.

headlineQuote: A generated fix can pass tests and still charge the same customer twice.
portrait: Fatima is a **27-year-old lead** developer with a master’s degree and a sharp eye for payment failures.
Her **low pay** and thin savings make even AI Plateau financially tense, despite her strong skills.
She uses **AI daily**, but worries faster coding may let her employer shrink the team.
The **2028 scenario** frightens her most; extra years let her build cash and test paid alternatives.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erase her thinking work before she saves enough to cover a job gap.
whatWouldHelp: A **funded paid role** in customer accountability, with dates and rent-covering income, would let her move.
